Egypt’s 2021 Avian Influenza Epidemic: Economic Impact Lingers in Retrospect

Cairo – Looking back three years, Egypt’s 2021 outbreak of avian influenza stands as one of the most significant public health crises in recent memory, with sweeping economic repercussions still being examined by industry experts. The epidemic, which struck in early spring, prompted the government to enact stringent national health measures, including temporary lockdowns, market closures, and the suspension of intercity transport for non-essential activities. These actions, though effective in curbing the spread of the virus, brought substantial economic disruption across sectors.

Among the affected firms was National Petroleum Co Ltd, which reported a sharp decline in fuel demand at the height of movement restrictions. “We experienced a 35% drop in local fuel distribution in the second quarter of 2021 compared to the previous year,” said Ahmed Saber, a spokesperson for the company. “With travel and industrial activity limited, our operations were scaled back significantly.”

The poultry industry, at the epicenter of the epidemic, faced the most immediate consequences, but the ripple effects extended to logistics, manufacturing, and retail. The Egyptian Chamber of Commerce estimated losses exceeding EGP 12 billion across these sectors. “It was a challenge for all businesses—large and small,” said Amal El-Sharif, an economic analyst. “Disruptions in supply chains, reduced workforce availability, and shifting consumer habits created a domino effect.”

In Alexandria, the port authority noted a temporary 22% reduction in cargo throughput, with petroleum products among the goods affected. “The movement restrictions meant less cargo coming in and out, especially fuel and related products,” said port manager Khaled Mostafa.

While Egypt has not faced such widespread closures since the epidemic, officials emphasize the importance of preparedness. “We learned valuable lessons about resilience and the need to safeguard both public health and economic activity,” said Dr. Hossam Abdelrahman, Deputy Minister of Health.

Today, there are no disruptions, but the legacy of 2021’s avian influenza outbreak continues to shape policy and industry strategy nationwide.
